★★★ THE RUNNABLE WITNESS FOR A FOUR-ROW MAPPING THAT SHIPPED INVERTED — D-ASM-ARM64-DIALECT-INVERTS-LDR-LDUR-MAPPING, shipped in `e5b60f6c` and corrected 2026-08-13.

★★★ WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG, AND WHY THE NAME OF A FIELD CAUSED IT. AArch64 gas spells four addressing forms — `ldr`/`str` are the SCALED unsigned-offset forms (imm12, scaled by the access size, reach 0..32760) and `ldur`/`stur` the UNSCALED signed ones (imm9, raw byte offset, reach -256..255). DSS's virtual ISA also has four opcodes, and the `_u` in `load_u`/`store_u` abbreviates **UNSIGNED-offset**, not **unscaled**. Read the other way — which is the natural reading — it points at exactly the opposite instruction, and the dialect paired all four rows backwards: `ldr→load`, `str→store`, `ldur→load_u`, `stur→store_u`.

★★ WHY IT SURVIVED A CYCLE AND A FULL GREEN SUITE: the failure was ASYMMETRIC. Writing `stur … #-8` elected the SCALED opcode, whose imm12 field is unsigned, so the encoder refused it LOUDLY (`A_ImmediateOperandOutOfRange`) — a build error nobody had a file to trigger. The other direction was the dangerous one and made no noise at all: a `ldr`/`str` routed to the UNSCALED encoder gets a well-formed instruction whose offset field is read as a raw byte count instead of a scaled one, i.e. the right instruction at the WRONG ADDRESS for every offset that is not a multiple of the access size.

★★★ WHY THE TWO HALVES USE DIFFERENT MAGNITUDES, WHICH IS THE WHOLE DESIGN OF THIS FILE. A round trip through one address proves nothing about which address it was — store and load agreeing is exactly as consistent when both are wrong. So each half picks an offset that ONLY ONE of the two encodings can represent, and each is verified through a SECOND, independently computed address:
  • HALF A (`stur x2, [x1, #-8]`) — negative, so the scaled form's UNSIGNED imm12 cannot carry it at all. Under the inverted rows this line does not assemble.
  • HALF B (`str x2, [x1, #512]`) — 512 is past the unscaled form's 255-byte reach, so under the inverted rows this line does not assemble either.
⇒ WITH THE FOUR ROWS SWAPPED BACK, THIS EXAMPLE DOES NOT BUILD. That is the red-on-disable arm, and it is a build failure rather than a wrong number because the encoders are already fail-loud on an unrepresentable immediate — the pin rides the diagnostic that already exists instead of a second one invented for it.

★★ AND THE EXIT CODE STILL CARRIES THE ADDRESS, not merely 'it compiled'. Both slots are POISONED FIRST through zero-displacement addressing (`[x4]`, `[x6]`, computed by `sub`/`add`), then written through the displaced form and read back through the poisoned route. A store that lands anywhere else leaves its poison intact and it shows up in the answer. The four outcomes are distinct — 70 correct · 156 half A misaddressed (100-200, truncated to a byte) · 43 half B misaddressed · 106 both — so a partial regression cannot read as a partial pass.

★ ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13 with the reference disassembler (`aarch64-linux-gnu-objdump`), because 'it exits 70' does not by itself say which encoding ran: `f81f8022 stur x2, [x1, #-8]` (unscaled, imm9) and `f9010022 str x2, [x1, #512]` (scaled — imm12 = 64 = 512/8, exactly the scaling the field requires). Both spellings also appear at offset 0 (`ldr x3, [x4]`, `ldur x7, [x6]`), so the pairing is exercised at both ends in both directions.

★ THE FRAME IS HAND-WRITTEN because that is what the `encode` tier means: `sub sp, sp, #1024` / `add sp, sp, #1024` is the programmer's own prologue and epilogue, and `materializeCallingConvention` does not run here by design. 1024 keeps sp 16-byte aligned and leaves x1-8 comfortably inside the frame. Only caller-saved registers are touched (x0-x7), so no AAPCS64 callee-saved register is clobbered and the trampoline's state survives.

★ THE `release` ARM, SCOPED HONESTLY. At the `encode` tier no MIR module exists, so the optimizer, the register allocator and calling-convention materialization never run — this arm does NOT witness the optimizer and cannot. It pins the narrower fact that `--config=release` still produces a working binary from assembly text.
